Yeah, and that's a very fair question. The Howie test was created by the courts to help determine the difference between a security and a commodity. We take the 200 cases at the circuit court level that have been used to further define the Howie test. We've read them all. and seeing the consistency in how the Howie test has been further refined over time and then take the cumulative work of those circuit courts and put it into the law. So no longer will the SEC be making a judgment call about whether something says security, the law will. And if something is unclear, then a legal challenge can be made using the Howie test and existing circuit court decisions to help iron those and resolve those types of questions.

So are you saying that you're going to legislate what the, I mean, I guess it won't be called the Howie Test anymore. You're going to legislate what a security is and how you read it within the laundry list of the Securities Exchange Act?

It will be using the existing Howie Test that is a court created definition, putting that definition into law, and then it will be more where we hope about those kinds of determinations, then it will still be up to the SEC to say, this fits the how he tested, this is a security, and then it would be up to the challenge of the digital asset that believes that SEC has got it wrong to prove in court that the SEC has got it wrong.
